title: When women journalists are silenced, the stories other women need disappear
subtitle: Journalists at a UN gathering called for faster protection and sustained support for women-led media. Their case reaches beyond newsroom safety: threats can cut communities off from information, education and a public record of abuse.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Women journalists and UN officials have called for emergency protection, stronger investigations into attacks and sustained funding for women-led reporting, warning that driving reporters out of conflict coverage also removes witnesses whose work communities depend on.
The 27 October event at UN headquarters in New York was organised by UNESCO, UN Women and Greece’s UN mission. The recommendations do not establish a new binding protection system.
“Every woman journalist driven out of a conflict zone is a peace process that loses its witness,” Maria Ressa said, according to UNESCO’s account.
What audiences lose

The consequences become concrete in Afghanistan, where Hamida Aman’s Begum media project has connected women and girls to educational broadcasting. In an August 2025 account, UNESCO described how Begum TV’s Tabasum programme transmitted from Paris into Afghan homes, combining learning with psychological support.

Its host, Diba Akbari, had left Afghanistan after losing her journalism job following the Taliban’s return. UNESCO reported her account of a ninth-grade girl who called the programme discouraged about online learning, then resumed studying after receiving encouragement from its psychologists. This was one reported experience, not an evaluation proving the programme’s overall effectiveness.

It nevertheless illustrates what can be at stake when a woman broadcaster loses the means to work. A newsroom can also be a route to practical knowledge, a place to ask a difficult question and a connection to people beyond the household. The public loss cannot be measured only by counting missing bylines.

Colombian journalist Jineth Bedoya, another participant in the New York discussion, offers a different example of journalism becoming a means of collective action. The World Association of News Publishers records her leadership of No Es Hora de Callar—It Is Not Time to Be Silent—a campaign against violence against women. Her work combines reporting with a sustained challenge to impunity, rather than asking survivors to carry the burden privately.
What the research can—and cannot—tell us

The warnings sit alongside evidence gathered for UN Women’s Tipping Point research. In its 2025 survey, 75 per cent of the 354 women journalists and media workers who answered the relevant question reported experiencing online violence in connection with their work. The finding was published in December 2025; it is not a new October 2026 measurement.

Researchers recruited participants through professional and civil-society networks, using purposive sampling and referrals. The survey ran from 27 August to 13 November 2025 in five languages. Its authors explicitly say the results cannot be generalised to the wider population. Participation varied between questions, and respondents’ accounts do not independently establish the cause of each incident.
Those qualifications matter. The figure describes the people who answered that question, not three-quarters of every woman working in journalism worldwide.

A further report in the series, summarised by UNESCO in May 2026, found that 45 per cent of surveyed women journalists and media workers reported censoring themselves on social media because of online violence; 22 per cent reported doing so at work. These findings describe a professional consequence as well as a personal one: a reporter may remain employed while becoming less able to speak freely.

They also complicate the familiar instruction to simply ignore abusive messages. Turning away from an account does not resolve a threat, protect a source or pay for legal assistance. Safety requires decisions by employers, platforms and public authorities.
Protection that lets women keep working

The New York panel’s recommendations included rapid emergency visas and relocation, legal assistance, confidential reporting channels and support reaching freelancers and local journalists. Participants also called for technology companies to answer coordinated harassment and for newsrooms to address sexual harassment within their own organisations.

The distinction between protecting someone and excluding her from work is crucial. Removing a woman from an assignment may reduce an employer’s immediate exposure while leaving her career, income and reporting relationships damaged. A credible response should give her workable options and a voice in decisions about her safety.

The next test is implementation: who will fund assistance, how quickly a threatened journalist can obtain it, and whether help reaches reporters without prominent employers or international recognition. The recommendations identify responsibilities; they do not demonstrate that those responsibilities have been met.

For audiences, the question is equally practical. When intimidation succeeds, which experiences become harder to document, which questions go unasked, and whose account of a conflict is left standing? Protecting women journalists means protecting the public’s ability to hear more than the voices already powerful enough to be heard.
The Athena Perspective.
